facts.title: A Name From the Dawn
facts.text: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word 'aurum', meaning 'shining dawn' or 'glow of sunrise'. Gold is one of the very few metals known to humanity since prehistoric times, with worked gold artifacts from the Varna necropolis in Bulgaria dating back about 6,500 years. Because it was never 'discovered' by a single person, no individual is credited with finding it.

facts.title: Born in Cosmic Collisions
facts.text: Most of the gold in the universe was forged not in ordinary stars but in violent events like neutron-star mergers and certain supernovae, where extreme neutron flux builds heavy nuclei. Astronomers confirmed this in 2017 when the GW170817 neutron-star collision, detected by LIGO, produced a glowing 'kilonova' rich in heavy elements. The gold in your jewelry literally predates the Earth and arrived in the cloud of dust that formed our planet.

facts.title: Almost Impossibly Unreactive
facts.text: Gold is famously a 'noble' metal: it does not rust, tarnish, or react with oxygen or most acids, which is why ancient gold coins emerge from shipwrecks still gleaming. It dissolves only in special mixtures such as aqua regia, a 3:1 blend of hydrochloric and nitric acid named 'royal water' because it could dissolve the king of metals. This chemical stability is the main reason gold has held value across thousands of years.

facts.title: Hammered Thinner Than Light
facts.text: Gold is the most malleable of all metals: a single gram can be beaten into a sheet covering about one square meter. Gold leaf can be made so thin, around 100 nanometers, that it becomes partly transparent and transmits a greenish-blue light. A single ounce of gold can be drawn into a wire roughly 80 kilometers long without breaking.

facts.title: Why Gold Looks Golden
facts.text: Almost all pure metals are silvery, but gold has a warm yellow color because of Einstein's relativity. Its electrons move so fast around the heavy nucleus that relativistic effects shift the light it absorbs into the blue range, so the reflected light appears golden. The same relativistic physics helps explain why neighboring mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

facts.title: Medicine Made of Metal
facts.text: Gold compounds called chrysotherapy, such as auranofin and sodium aurothiomalate, were used for decades to treat rheumatoid arthritis by calming inflammation. Today, tiny gold nanoparticles are being developed to carry cancer drugs and to heat and destroy tumors when struck by infrared light. Radioactive gold-198 has even been used directly in some cancer treatments.

facts.title: The Metal Inside Your Phone
facts.text: Gold is an outstanding electrical conductor that never corrodes, so it is plated onto connectors, circuit boards, and SIM cards in nearly every smartphone and computer. Roughly 7 to 50 milligrams of gold sit inside a typical mobile phone, which is why 'urban mining' of electronic waste can be richer than digging real ore. A tonne of discarded phones can yield more gold than a tonne of mined rock.

facts.title: Dissolved Across the Oceans
facts.text: Earth's seawater contains an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes of dissolved gold, but it is spread so thinly, only parts per trillion, that no one has found a profitable way to extract it. In the 1920s the German chemist Fritz Haber, a Nobel laureate, spent years trying to harvest sea gold to pay World War I reparations, and ultimately failed. The vast majority of usable gold instead sits locked in rock deep underground.

facts.title: Edible and Officially Safe
facts.text: Because gold is so unreactive, pure gold leaf is biologically inert and approved as a food additive in Europe under the code E175. It passes through the body without being absorbed, so the flakes on luxury desserts and the gold in some liqueurs add sparkle but no flavor or nutrition. It has no known biological role in humans, which is exactly why it can be eaten safely.

facts.title: Guarding Spacecraft and Astronauts
facts.text: Gold reflects infrared radiation extremely well, so a thin gold coating shields satellites and astronauts' helmet visors from intense solar heat and glare. The visors on Apollo lunar helmets and the sunshield on the James Webb Space Telescope both rely on gold films just micrometers thick. The same reflective property makes gold valuable for protecting sensitive electronics in the harsh environment of space.
